identity.title: Actions Speak Louder than Prompts: A Large-Scale Study of LLMs for Graph Inference

problem.claim: Characterize how LLMs perform on text-rich graph tasks, especially node classification, across interaction modes and graph conditions.

gap.claim: The field lacks a principled understanding of LLM capabilities for processing graph data.

contributions.claim: A large-scale, controlled evaluation varying interaction mode, graph domain, homophily, text length, LLM size, and reasoning capability.
An analysis of reliance on features, edges, and labels through independent truncation or deletion.
Actionable conclusions about the strengths, limitations, and future design principles of LLM–graph interaction modes.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a large-scale controlled study spanning multiple LLM–graph interaction modes and graph conditions, with targeted input-dependency analysis.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that code generation has the strongest overall performance, with especially large gains on long-text or high-degree graphs where prompting quickly exceeds the token budget.
The authors report that all interaction strategies remain effective on heterophilic graphs, challenging the assumption that LLM-based methods collapse under low homophily.
The authors report that code generation can shift reliance toward whichever input type—structure, features, or labels—is most informative.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs are increasingly used for text-rich graph tasks, including high-impact node classification applications.
The authors identify a lack of principled understanding of LLM graph-processing capabilities.
They conduct a controlled evaluation across interaction modes, graph regimes, domains, text lengths, model sizes, reasoning capabilities, and input dependencies.
They report advantages for code generation, continued effectiveness under heterophily, and adaptive reliance on informative inputs.

source_observation.claim: The study varies interaction mode and graph conditions jointly, then separately removes or truncates input types.

lessons.interpretation: Factorized evaluation can reveal when a method’s apparent advantage depends on particular data regimes or inputs.
lessons.application: Report results in a matrix crossing interaction mode with graph regime, text length, degree, and input ablations.
lessons.exception: This may be unsuitable when the task lacks enough data or compute to support controlled factorial comparisons.

source_observation.claim: The reported code-generation advantage is qualified by long-text and high-degree settings, while prompting may exceed the token budget.

lessons.interpretation: Method claims become more informative when tied to concrete operational constraints and failure conditions.
lessons.application: State the regime and resource constraint under which a proposed method is expected to outperform alternatives.
lessons.exception: Avoid this framing when no meaningful regime-specific mechanism or constraint has been identified.

unknowns: The abstract gives no dataset sizes, model identities or sizes, metrics, baselines, statistical uncertainty, or numerical results.
The meaning of “effective” across heterophilic graphs and the conditions behind adaptive input reliance are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish independently verified validity, reproducibility, or priority of the stated novelty.
